content: In 1999, the company was referred to as The pharmacy of the world due to its significant role in the global pharmaceutical market. The company was originally established in 1863 under the name Teerfarbenfabrik Meister, Lucius & Co. in Höchst, near Frankfurt. It later changed its name to Teerfarbenfabrik Meister Lucius & Brüning. By 1880, it transitioned into a stock company named Farbwerke vorm. Meister Lucius & Brüning AG. For international markets, the name was simplified to Farbwerke Hoechst AG. Until 1925, Hoechst AG operated independently. Hoechst AG was one of the co-founders of IG Farben, a conglomerate formed in 1916 as a coalition of Germany's chemical industry to consolidate industrial power during and after World War I. In 1925, IG Farben transitioned from a pressure group into a well-known conglomerate. However, IG Farben was dissolved in 1951, and its founding companies were re-established. Hoechst AG was re-founded on December 7, 1951, in Frankfurt, with an initial capitalization of 100,000 Deutsche Mark. In 1987, Hoechst acquired the American chemical company Celanese and established a new U.S. subsidiary, Hoechst Celanese. However, there was a boycott of all Hoechst pharmaceutical products, including Altace, by certain groups in the United States. These groups encouraged consumers to focus on key Hoechst drugs with significant economic impact rather than adopting a broad boycott approach. Altace was specifically listed as a product to boycott. At the time, Altace generated less than $90 million in revenue for Hoechst, and the company had ceased promoting it within the U.S. market. In 1997, Hoechst underwent a major restructuring, transferring its various business units to independent companies, such as Nutrinova and Clariant. The company then narrowed its focus to prescription drugs under its subsidiary Hoechst Marion Roussel (HMR), including Allegra, Cardizem, Seldane, Claforan, Lasix, DiaBeta, and Nicoderm. Notably, Altace was no longer included in the list of boycotted products by Concerned Women for America. On December 18, 1998, King Pharmaceuticals, through its wholly-owned subsidiary Monarch Pharmaceuticals, acquired the distribution rights to Altace and other Hoechst products from Hoechst Marion Roussel, a subsidiary of Hoechst AG based in Kansas City, Missouri. Following a merger, the newly formed company was headquartered in Strasbourg, France. As part of this merger, Hoechst divested many of its industrial businesses into Celanese, which subsequently became an independent company once again.
